column3: In 2Pet.1.8 ἀργός shifts from its base 'idle/unemployed' gloss to a metaphorical 'ineffective' sense applied to spiritual qualities, paired with ἄκαρπος ('unfruitful') -- the nuance here is qualitative barrenness of Christian character rather than literal non-labor. column3: Yes, the mechanism differs by context. In G0692 (Matt.20.3/6) the mechanism is circumstantial/economic -- absence of an employer's summons. In 1Tim.5.13/Titus.1.12 (G0692, cluster context) idleness operates via habitual moral choice leading to further vice. In H8220 (Eccl.10.18) the mechanism is physical/instrumental -- slack hands failing to maintain a structure, producing direct material decay. In G0691 (2Pet.2.3) the 'mechanism' is rhetorical/theological -- a personification denying dormancy to underscore the certainty of divine judgment's operation. Four distinct registers (economic, moral, physical, theological-rhetorical) for the same root concept.

column3: Luke.18.11 and Luke.17.16 form a notable contrast within G2168's own occurrence list despite sharing surface/morph similarity (both are personal, individual, first/third-person verb forms of direct address): the Pharisee's 'I thank you, God' (Luke.18.11) is self-congratulatory and comparison-driven ('that I am not like other men'), while the Samaritan leper's 'giving him thanks' (Luke.17.16) is embodied, physical (falling at Jesus' feet), and offered by a social outsider. Both are individual, spontaneous (non-epistolary, non-liturgical-formula) uses of the same verb, showing the strong's range stretches to cover both a distorted, self-referential invocation of thanksgiving-language and a genuine, humble enactment of it -- an internal polarity visible only by setting these two occurrences against each other and against the epistolary/meal-formula groups.
